about: The frigate's anchors and cables (docs/shipkit-10): the bower anchors catted and fished at the catheads, the sheet and stream anchors and the kedges, the catheads, the hawse holes, the billboards and the hemp cables. Metres in the ship's frame (X forward, Y starboard, Z up, origin on the centreline at midships on waterline A) unless a key says ft, in or lb. Starboard parts are mirrored for port where a key says so. Every size is the period's practice for a 44 (an estimate) unless its src gives a source.

sources.fact_file: US Navy fact file for USS Constitution: two bower anchors of 5,300 lb, a sheet anchor of 5,400 lb, a stream anchor of 1,100 lb and two kedges of 400 to 700 lb (as quoted by the searches; the page itself is on a host this machine cannot open)
sources.museum_cable: USS Constitution Museum: her anchor cables were 22 in round (September 1797); four hawse pipes in her bows today, cast iron of the 1870s; whether the holes were lined with lead in her early years is not known, but some protective lining is likely
sources.draught_1817: the 1817 draught of a 44 (refs.json): the cathead over the rail at the head rail's after end, rising about 40 degrees as seen from the side, a carved cat's face on its end
sources.rig_plan: the later rig plan (refs.json, p72): two hawse holes a side between the cheeks, under the upper cheek
sources.period_tables: anchor tables of the 1780s-1800s as quoted in modellers' notes (the books' own hosts are blocked here): an 81 cwt anchor's shank 19 ft 8 in, a 29.5 cwt anchor's 13 ft 8 in; the shank three times the arm; the stock as long as the shank and half the ring's diameter; best bower forward on the fore channel, the sheet anchor on the channel abaft it, the spare abaft the small bower on the other side; the bill of the inner fluke rests on the billboard when the anchor is fished
sources.practice: the period's practice for a large frigate, by eye where no drawing or table gives it (each so marked)
sources.rnli_1800: RNLI, The Lifeboat journal, 'Anchors: old forms and recent developments' (as quoted by the searches): an anchor of about 1800 had a 19 ft shank, a 21 ft stock and 12 ft from pea to pea, its palms taking up nearly half the arm's length
sources.admiralty_ratios: the Admiralty's proportions for an anchor as quoted on a modellers' forum (unverified; the host is blocked here): the shank three times the arm, the arm 60 degrees off the shank, the palm's base and the ring's outside diameter each four times the trend (the shank's thickness at the throat), the palm an inch or so longer than it is broad

iron_src: wrought iron, 7,600 to 7,850 kg/m3; an anchor's weight is its iron (shank, arms, palms and ring), the wooden stock left out, as the period quoted it

sheet.src: fact_file; stowed outside on the starboard side abaft the fore chains, where the period stowed it (period_tables; slice 12, Bean's choice, Nov 16: sheet_stow). Laid on the fore channel itself it would lie across the forecastle's foremost carronade port and the chase port there, so it lies under the channel's level, abaft its end

stream.src: fact_file; with the boats in the waist (slice 11; Bean's choice, Nov 15), not in the spare anchor's place on the channel abaft the small bower (period_tables), for the same ports

kedge_large.src: fact_file (the larger of the two); with the boats, the launch carrying them out to kedge (slice 11)

shape.shank_src: period_tables: 4.55 and 4.43 ft per cube root of the weight in cwt for the two anchors quoted; 4.5 gives the bowers 16.3 ft, the sheet 16.4, the stream 9.6, the kedges 8.3 and 6.9
shape.arm_src: practice: each arm struck on a radius of about a third of the shank from a centre on it (0.36 of the shank), through about a radian, so the bills stand about 60 degrees off the shank and pea to pea is 0.6 of the shank (10 ft for the bowers); its length along the arc 0.36 of the shank (period_tables: about a third)
shape.palm_src: rnli_1800: the palm (fluke) nearly half the arm long (0.48 of it); admiralty_ratios: about as broad as it is long (0.95); practice: a plate on the arm's inner face, square across its back end (toward the crown) with rounded shoulders, widest 0.3 of its length out from that end, its sides curving in to its point at the bill, thickest on the arm
shape.throat_solved: the shank's side at the throat is solved so the iron weighs the anchor's weight (anchors.Anchor.solve): every section scales with it
shape.section_src: practice: the shank square with its edges taken off, tapering to 0.62 of the throat under the stock, curved into the arms' tops at the throat on a radius of 0.45 of the throat's side; the arms 0.95 of it at the crown, 0.66 at the palm and 0.4 at the bill; the palm 0.3 of the throat thick on the arm, its rim 0.35 of that
shape.ring_src: practice between the sources: the ring's outside diameter 0.18 of the shank (the stock's rule with rnli_1800's 19 ft shank and 21 ft stock gives 0.21, admiralty_ratios' four times the trend about 0.19; the bowers' ring 2.9 ft), its bar 0.022 of the shank (4.3 in for the bowers)
shape.pudden_src: practice: a bower's ring puddened (wrapped with old rope against the cable's chafe), 1.5 in thick; the small anchors' rings bare
shape.stock_src: period_tables: the stock as long as the shank and half the ring's diameter; practice: a twelfth of its length square in the middle, tapering on its lower face and its sides to half at the ends, its top straight; two oak pieces bolted round the shank's square with a gap of an inch between them, under four iron hoops (two a side, 0.09 and 0.2 of the stock's length out from the middle, 4 by 3/4 in); two nuts on the shank under it

cable.lay_src: practice: cable-laid (three ropes laid up left-handed), a lay about three times the cable's thickness
cable.via_src: estimate: corners of the cable's course up the bow from the hawse hole to the ring, clear of the bolster, the cheeks, the planking, the shank painter and the bowsprit's rigging
cable.bore_out_src: estimate: the cable comes out of the hole along its bore, lying on the lining toward its pull, and turns up the bow on its arc from a corner this far out past the mouth (0.38 until slice 12; since then the cable comes in from the gun deck across the bore and bends a few degrees over the outer lip as well, and that bend's arc shares this straight with the turn up the bow)
cable.bend_src: practice: a cable-laid cable is stiff; each turn of its course is an arc of at least one and a half times its thickness (the build fails on a tighter one outside the clinch)
cable.tail_src: practice: the clinch's end about two feet past the eye's throat, seized to the standing part with two seizings; the standing part lies straight alongside it all the way and lead_m past its end (estimate)

plug.src: practice: at sea the holes with no cable in them are stopped with hawse plugs, an oak plug driven in from inboard (its head, head_in[0] thick, reaching head_in[1] past the lining onto the inner lip; the plug length_in long, tapering to taper of its diameter); the bucklers outside are left off (estimate)

hawse.src: rig_plan: two holes a side between the cheeks, under the upper cheek ((x, z) where each bore's axis meets the moulded hull, the frames' outside, ship: the mouths on the planking come out about 0.1 m forward of these); practice: an 11 in bore for a 7 in cable, each hole bored aft, a little inboard (axis_deg: the bore's turn inboard of fore and aft, and its rise inboard), lined with lead lapped over its mouth (lip_in) a lead_in thick, in a bolster (an oak pad round both holes) standing bolster_proud_m off the planking, bolster_margin_m round the holes and let into the planking bolster_embed_m; the mouths as high under the upper cheek as leaves the bolster clear of it; the bores cut through cut_parts (the planking and, slice 12, the gun deck's side: each bore runs through to the side's inner face and is lined all the way, its lining's lip lapped over the inner mouth as over the outer; until slice 12 each ended capped a quarter metre inside the planking)

cathead.src: draught_1817: the cathead over the rail at the head rail's after end, rising about 40 degrees as seen from the side (ours, its centre over the rail at rail_x, stands about half a metre forward of our head rails' after ends, x 24.4 to 24.5); practice: 55 degrees off fore and aft in plan and a 27 degree steeve (40 degrees as the side sees it), 15 in square at the rail and 13.5 by 14 in at the end, standing out_m past the rail cap's outer edge, let into the cap and the bulwark's top and bolted through them, its heel cut off at the bulwark's inner face (heel_proud_m proud of it: the pin rail and the coils under it leave no room for a heel on the deck or an inboard knee); no supporter under it outboard, where the headsail sheets' blocks hang (practice would give it a knee there); three sheaves in its end for the cat fall, end_block_m of solid timber outboard of them (room for the cat stopper's hole); the cat's face carved on the end (draught_1817)

fished.src: practice: catted (the ring hove up close under the cathead's sheaves by the cat and held there by the cat stopper) and fished (the inner fluke's bill brought to the billboard on the bow by the fish tackle, the shank painter passed round the shank); the anchor hangs about the line from its eye to that bill as its weight takes it (roll_from_natural_deg turns it further). The bow from the cathead to the fore chains is about 13 ft and the bower's shank 16 ft, so she cannot lie fished flat along the side: laid flatter, her crown and arms come down across the foremost gun deck port, whose lid opens 175 deg and whose gun runs out 24 deg forward (docs/shipkit-8), or into the fore chains. bill_x: between that port and the bridle port, where she hangs clear of both (docs/shipkit-10)

billboard.src: practice: an oak board on the bow where the bill of the inner fluke rests, faced with an iron plate (plate_margin_m in from the board's edge), centred under the bill, bent to the bow and let into the planking embed_m; as thick as brings the plate's face to the bill (about thick_in: anchors.json says how thick)

stopper.src: practice: the cat (ring) stopper, a rope with a wall knot in its end rove down through a hole in the cathead's end, through the bower's ring under its bar (the ring hangs on it) and up again inboard of the sheaves; the period's stopper 'is attached to the cat-head, passes through the anchor ring, and is afterwards fastened to the timber-head' (Encyclopaedia Britannica, 1815, as quoted by the searches; its host is blocked here), belayed there so the anchor can be let go: ours takes its hauling end up through a second hole hole_in_m inboard of the sheaves' slots and knots it on the cathead's top like the other (simplified); a 44's stopper about 4.5 in
stopper.hole_src: estimate: each hole square through the cathead, hole_gap_in clear of the rope all round; each leg turns into its hole turn_below_m under the cathead on a bend_m radius
stopper.knot_src: estimate: a wall knot about knot_of_diameter [across, high] rope diameters (a single wall knot, crowned, in three-strand rope)

painter.eye_src: estimate: each eyebolt's eye [its centre-line diameter, its bar, the shank] in, big enough for the rope's splice to pass through it round the bar, standing square to the rope's lead; the splice's throat throat_m out from the bar, its end tucked back splice_m along the standing part, splice_gap_in clear of the iron
painter.src: practice: the shank painter (a rope here; large ships' were often part chain) from an eyebolt in the bow rise_m above where it takes the shank (at_shank of the eye's height up from the crown), a round turn about the shank and back up to an eyebolt beside the first, each end spliced round its eyebolt

sheet_stow.src: practice (Bean's choice, Nov 16): the sheet anchor stowed outside on the starboard side abaft the fore chains (Steel 1794 stows the sheet anchors at the after part of the fore shrouds). Its eye is forward, the ring turned toward the fore channel and lashed with lash_turns turns of lash_circ_in rope (lash_m between the ring's bar and the eyebolt's eye) to an eyebolt in the channel's after end, out_m out from the side. It is turned about its shank until the bill of its inner fluke rests on a billboard (as the bowers': bill_off_m off the planking) and the lower end of its stock bears on the side (stock_gap_m off it): the roll and how far the shank lies out are solved together. Its stock is long (17.85 ft) and stands nearly up and down: the shank lies so high that the anchor's lowest point, the stock's lower end, stands heel_clear_m over the sea with the ship heeled heel_deg to starboard (a working heel; the stock's foot no longer dips at 8 deg). The waist's side is low here (its plankshear about 0.8 m over the gun deck lids' hinges, the open rail on stanchions above it), and the bill must stay bill_under_top_m under the moulding for its billboard (moved down the side from under the bill until its top is half an inch under the moulding): so the shank rises forward from its crown, low over the billboard, to its eye at the channel, as little as both need (no more than max_slope_deg), and passes shank_over_hinges_m over the hinges of every lid whose span (clear_of_lids_in beyond its edges) it crosses, so the lids open under it. A shank painter (as the bowers', but of circ_in rope: the sheet anchor's is the heavier and its legs the flatter) takes her weight from two eyebolts driven up into the waist rail's cap (in_from_edge_in in from its outer edge, into_in into it, clear of its stanchions), as high over the shank as the side reaches here: its legs lead up at about 40 to 44 deg (the shank stands 1.5 m out, where the stock's foot bears on the wales), so each would carry about 0.75 of her weight were it to take all of it, and the rope is sized for that at min_safety times under its breaking strain (break_tons_per_circ2 times its circumference squared, in long tons: a rule for good hemp; checked). Its legs run from the shank up past the lids, and a lid swings out and up across its own span fore and aft, so the painter comes down between two lids: in the stretch of the shank clear of every lid (clear_of_lids_in beyond its edges, an estimate), the billboard and the stock by its own reach, the one whose middle is nearest at_shank of the eye's height up from the crown, at its middle (anchors.json sheet.painter says where)

meets.note: the anchors' parts that meet another part of the ship (or each other) by design, each pair with why and how far (in) either may go into the other; every other meeting fails the build (build_frigate's anchors_room, deck.room). Each entry: the parts on one side, the parts on the other, why, the depth allowed: the deepest the build measures over the entry's pairs (deck.room's measure, how far a vertex lies behind the other's nearest face, found within 0.3 m, so never more than 11.8 in) with a quarter inch over, a guard against a part moving deeper. A designed contact the build no longer finds fails it too: a part meant to be driven into, let into or resting on another that no longer reaches it hangs clear of what holds it
pairs: the cathead is let into the rail cap and bolted through it
the cathead is let into the bulwark's top under the rail cap
the cathead's heel is cut off just inside the bulwark's inner face, its sides passing through that face
the stopper is rove through the bower's ring and takes its weight under the bar
the billboard is bent to the bow and let into the planking
the bill of the bower's inner fluke rests on the billboard's iron plate
the hawse bolster is bent to the bow and let into the planking
the lead linings fill the bolster's holes and are lapped over its face
the hawse holes' lead linings run in through the side and are lapped over its inner face on the gun deck (slice 12)
an oak plug is driven from inboard into each hawse hole that has no cable in it, through its lining, its head on the lining's inner lip (slice 12)
the shank painters' eyebolts are driven into the bow
the painter's round turn bears on the shank
the sheet anchor's billboard is bent to the side and let into the planking
the bill of the sheet anchor's inner fluke rests on its billboard's iron plate
the sheet anchor's painter eyebolts are driven up into the waist rail's cap
the sheet anchor's lashing eyebolt is driven into the fore channel's after end
the sheet anchor's painter's round turn bears on its shank
the sheet anchor's lashing is passed round its ring's bar
the sheet anchor's lashing is rove through its eyebolt's eye in the fore channel
